transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-04-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Alex Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Kumar (Sunrise Head of ML), Ethan Brooks (Sunrise Infra Lead), Sofia Martinez (Sunrise CTO)

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll go about 45ish minutes, try to leave time for next steps. Quick intros?
[00:00:09] Priya Kumar: Hi, Priya here, lead ML at Sunrise. We own the chat assistant and the recommendation prompt pipelines.
[00:00:14] Ethan Brooks: Ethan, infra, I look after cluster, VPC and security.
[00:00:17] Sofia Martinez: Sofia, CTO, jumping in for high level and timeline alignment.
[00:00:22] Alex Ruiz: Alex, I'm the SE on Redwood side, I'll dive into sizing and the fallback mech.
[00:00:26] Maya Chen: Great. Purpose — scoping the POC for capacity sizing and autoscale: reserved GPUs for baseline, burst pattern, and circuit-breaker fallback policies.

Summary and context exchange
[00:01:02] Priya Kumar: Our main success criteria: p95 latency under 450ms for short chat (<=128 tokens), p99 under 900ms ideally. Cost ceiling is about 30% less than our current cloud vendor spend, else execs will balk. Also quality mustn't degrade more than 2% on our prompt set.
[00:01:28] Sofia Martinez: Timeline: we want a pilot ready in ~3 weeks, not a multi-month POC. So scoping needs to be tight.
[00:01:37] Maya Chen: Ok noted. Alex, can you lay out how we think about reserved + burst sizing?

Workload sizing & reserved baseline
[00:02:00] Alex Ruiz: Sure. First, we need a representative traffic trace. Ideally 7-14 days with timestamps, request sizes, model types, and tail percentiles. From that we calculate baseline RPS and the 95/99 bursts. For reserved GPU commit we size to cover baseline sustained load with room for cache hit savings — Redwood uses prefix caching and KV cache to reduce repeated context work, that usually buys you 10-40% token savings depending on prompt variety.
[00:02:34] Priya Kumar: Quick flag — our prompts are medium-churn: around 30% repeat prefixes, but many dynamic user messages.
[00:02:41] Alex Ruiz: OK that pushes the expected cache hit to the lower end. For GPUs, if you're using an Llama-style 13B quantized on A100-equivalent, baseline of 40 concurrent requests (avg 80 tokens) maps to roughly 2-3 reserved GPUs for steady-state with efficient batching. Bursts above that we'd route to burst pool or fall back to cheaper variant.
[00:03:05] Ethan Brooks: When you say cheaper variant, what do you mean operationally? Is that like switching to a 7B quantized copy?
[00:03:12] Alex Ruiz: Exactly, a model variant in the catalog — same API, different model id. We can do weighted rollbacks, circuit-breaker triggers.

Benchmark plan and metrics
[00:03:30] Maya Chen: Benchmarks — we'll run two phases: dry-run synthetic to verify baseline numbers, then joint replay of their traffic trace to validate p95/p99 and cost. Metrics: latency percentiles, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, queue depth, and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:03:49] Priya Kumar: We also want quality checks — automated evals against our prompt set, track hallucination or relevance drop.
[00:03:56] Alex Ruiz: We'll integrate eval harness to run in parallel. Note: quantization or switching model families can shift semantic quality; we'll capture that.

Burst strategy and queueing
[00:04:20] Alex Ruiz: For bursts, recommended pattern is reserved pool for baseline, a small warm buffer pool (reserved but spun-down) and then a burst-on-demand pool. Two levers: 1) short-lived burst nodes spun via reserved burst capacity in regions, and 2) warm standby with fast startup for critical low-latency lanes. Queueing policy: prioritize in-flight sessions and small requests to keep latency SLOs.
[00:04:47] Ethan Brooks: How fast are warm startups? If we need extra GPUs during a spike, what's the cold start?
[00:04:52] Alex Ruiz: Cold start from zero can be 30-90s depending on image pull and model load. Warm standby reduces to sub-10s for quantized models if the VM and cached image are ready. So we model ramp with a short buffer and circuit-breaker to avoid overwhelming.

Circuit-breaker and fallback policies
[00:05:15] Maya Chen: Let's go through an example policy: if queue depth > X or p99 > Y ms for 2 consecutive 30s windows, trigger circuit-breaker route to fallback model variant (cheaper) and optionally region failover. After stabilization, do gradual ramp-down back to primary.
[00:05:34] Priya Kumar: What's a sensible X/Y? For us maybe queue depth > 150 or p99 > 1500ms triggers.
[00:05:41] Alex Ruiz: That seems reasonable as a start. For p95 target you mentioned 450ms, p99 900ms, so a 1500ms trip threshold gives headroom. We'll provide recommended thresholds in the runbook.

Cost controls and ROI
[00:06:05] Sofia Martinez: We need a cost model. If fallback to cheaper model increases user dissatisfaction, we need to measure business impact. How do we present unit economics?
[00:06:13] Maya Chen: We'll produce cost per 1k tokens across reserved vs burst vs fallback. Also show CPU/GPU unit-hours. Redwood Optimize will simulate cost impact of different batching and quantization profiles.
[00:06:25] Priya Kumar: Also, show breakout of data egress, networking if we cross regions.

Security and private constraints
[00:06:40] Ethan Brooks: For POC, we require VPC peering or PrivateLink, SAML SSO, and audit logs. We also need encryption-at-rest KMS controls when in private deployment. Can Redwood replicate logs to our SIEM?
[00:06:52] Alex Ruiz: Yes, we support VPC peering and private control plane for Private deployments. Audit logs can be forwarded via syslog/S3 and KMS/HSM integrations are supported. For the pilot we'll use a secure tunnel and token scoping; in the runbook we'll capture exact integration steps.

Risks and mitigation
[00:07:12] Maya Chen: Call out risks: long cold starts, quality regression on fallback, data residency. Mitigations: warm buffer nodes, A/B evaluation on fallback variants, region-aware routing.
[00:07:25] Priya Kumar: If fallback causes >2% drop in quality, we need instant rollback. Can the circuit-breaker do auto-rollback?
[00:07:30] Alex Ruiz: Yes, we support auto-fallback but the safe pattern is gradual rollback with small percentage traffic canary to monitor quality metrics then full cutover. We'll codify that.

Plan and timeline
[00:07:50] Maya Chen: Proposed timeline: this week collect traces and infra contacts; next week Redwood builds runbook and runs synthetic bench; week of 4/24 joint replay and benchmarks; by end of that week deliver final POC report. That matches your 3-week ask.
[00:08:06] Sofia Martinez: That works for execs. I want an initial cost estimate before the joint bench though.
[00:08:11] Maya Chen: We'll send estimate along with runbook.

Closing recap and explicit next steps
[00:08:30] Maya Chen: Recap: Send runbook & pricing (Redwood), Sunrise provides traces and infra constraints, schedule benchmark slot week of 4/24. Action items will be emailed. Anything else?
[00:08:43] Priya Kumar: Add an item to include sample responses from fallback model to review quality delta.
[00:08:48] Alex Ruiz: Good call — we'll include automated eval diffs and sample artifacts.
[00:08:52] Ethan Brooks: I'll share our security contact and VPC CIDR ranges.
[00:08:55] Sofia Martinez: Thank you, looking forward.

[00:09:00] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the runbook and draft pricing.

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard tokens: "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K V cash"; product names like "Redwood Private" sometimes shown as "read would private" in quick speech. There was a 10 second mute at ~00:04:40 where Ethan reconnected.

End of transcript.
